title: A Cornish Conundrum
bodyHtml:
Cornish (known in Cornish as Kernewek) is the Celtic language of the county of Cornwall (Kernow) in South West England. It stopped being actively spoken in the late 1700s, but knowledge of the language survived, and since the early 1900s, attempts have been made to revive it. Currently, there is a growing number of second language speakers, as well as some children who are being brought up speaking Cornish.

I3. Some people believe that the English word for a certain animal comes from a phrase meaning "white head" in Welsh, a language that is closely related to Cornish. What is this animal? Write your answer in English.

questions.partPrompt: Complete the table by filling in the gaps with the correct Cornish words. For the singular English word "frog", the definite singular is "the frog", the plural is "frogs", and the definite plural is "the frogs".
Fill in the blanks in the table.

Some people believe that the English word for a certain animal comes from a phrase meaning "white head" in Welsh, a language that is closely related to Cornish. What is this animal? Write your answer in English.

hints.text: Compare the first letter of each word across the four columns of the big table. Sometimes it stays the same, sometimes it changes in a regular way: b and v, d and dh, k and g, m and v, p and b, t and d, gw and w. Make a list of these pairs before you try to fill anything in.

The consonant change (a "mutation") is triggered by grammar, not by sound alone. Work out which forms trigger it: think about the gender of the noun (feminine or masculine), whether the noun refers to a person, and whether the little word war ‘on’ comes in front. Adjectives can be mutated too, by the noun in front of them. Since the plain singular is never mutated, you can use the mutated forms as clues to reconstruct it, and vice versa.

Take the row for ‘girl’: mowes, an vowes, mowysi, an mowysi. The m of mowes becomes v only in the definite singular, which tells you the noun is feminine; the definite plural is left alone. Compare gwarier ‘male actor’, where the mutation instead shows up in the definite plural an warioryon, because that noun is masculine and refers to a person. Those two rows give you the two halves of the rule.

explanationHtml:
What is going on with these first letters?

Look along the rows of the first table and watch only the initial consonant. Sometimes all four forms start with the same letter (kwilkyn, an kwilkyn, kwilkynyow, an kwilkynyow), and sometimes one form is the odd one out (benyn but an venyn). Collecting the odd ones out gives a fixed set of swaps, which Celtic languages call a soft mutation (a regular change to the first sound of a word, caused by grammar):

  • b becomes v
  • d becomes dh
  • gw becomes w
  • k becomes g
  • m becomes v
  • p becomes b
  • t becomes d

Notice that the bare singular column is never mutated. So the bare singular is your "safe" form, and any mutated form can be turned back by undoing one of the swaps above.

When does the mutation happen?

Now sort the rows by where the change appears.

Mutation in the definite singular only. benyn / an venyn ‘woman’, kares / an gares ‘girlfriend’, davas / an dhavas ‘sheep’, mowes / an vowes ‘girl’, pluven / an bluven ‘pen’. These are all feminine nouns. Rule: feminine nouns mutate after an in the singular.

Mutation in the definite plural only. gwarioryon / an warioryon ‘male actors’, pennsevigyon / an bennsevigyon ‘princes’, tiogow / an diogow ‘male farmers’. These are masculine and they all refer to people. Compare ponsyow ‘bridges’ and gweliow ‘beds’, which are masculine but not people: no mutation. Rule: masculine nouns mutate in the definite plural only when they refer to people.

Feminine nouns never mutate in the plural (an benenes, an karesow, an deves, an mowysi), and masculine non-person nouns never mutate at all after an.

Using the rule to fill the gaps in I1

Each blank is solved by asking two questions: is the noun feminine or masculine, and does it refer to a person?

  • dama / an dhama shows the mutation d-to-dh in the definite singular, so ‘mother’ is feminine. Feminine plurals are not mutated, so the definite plural just adds an.
  • For ‘mare’ we are given an gasek. Undo k-to-g and you recover the bare singular. The definite plural an kasegi is unmutated (feminine, and not a person), so the bare plural is the same word without an.
  • ‘King’ gives an vyghternedh in the definite plural, which is m-to-v: masculine, refers to people. So the definite singular of a masculine noun keeps its m. ‘Queen’ behaves the mirror way: feminine, so the singular mutates and the plural does not.
  • tas ‘father’: masculine and a person, so the plural tasow gets t-to-d after an, while the singular stays put. Likewise maw ‘boy’, whose definite plural an vebyon hides the unmutated plural under v-to-m.
  • bogh ‘billy-goat’, badh ‘boar’, tarow ‘bull’, kulyek ‘cockerel’ are masculine animals, not people, so nothing mutates and the columns are straightforward. banow ‘sow’ is feminine, so only its definite singular mutates.

The second table: war and adjectives

Two more triggers show up in the phrase list.

Everything mutates after war ‘on’. pons becomes war bons, davas becomes war dhavas, tesennow becomes war desennow, gweliow becomes war weliow, krogen becomes war grogen. Gender and number make no difference here.

Adjectives mutate after a feminine singular noun, or after a plural masculine human noun. Compare war bons perfydh ‘on a perfect bridge’ (masculine singular: the adjective keeps its p) with war bluven berfydh ‘on a perfect pen’ (feminine singular: perfydh becomes berfydh) and war vyghternedh berfydh ‘on perfect kings’ (masculine plural people: mutated again). This is how you can tell a noun's gender even when you have never seen its definite form: pal drosek ‘noisy spade’ has a mutated adjective (trosek becomes drosek), so pal is feminine, whereas an bal byhan ‘the small mine’ has an unmutated adjective, so that bal is a different, masculine word.

Working out I2

‘Finger’ comes from bys bras ‘thumb’ and bys byhan ‘pinky finger’, so the word is bys. Nothing in the data suggests it is feminine, so the definite singular just adds the article unchanged.

‘On a beautiful cake’ needs three steps: the singular of ‘cake’ (recovered from an desen), then the mutation caused by war, then the mutation of the adjective teg ‘beautiful’ because the noun is feminine singular; compare war dhas deg ‘on a beautiful stack’.

‘On a door’ takes daras (seen in penn daras and daras melyn) and applies the d-to-dh mutation after war.

Going the other way, an bal berfydh has a mutated adjective, so the noun is feminine: this is pal ‘spade’, not the masculine bal ‘mine’. And das is the unmutated form behind war dhas deg, so it means ‘stack’; while war das must be a mutated t-word, so its base form is tas.

I3: the white-headed animal

Gather every colour word in the problem: glas ‘blue’, glasrudh ‘purple’, rudhvelyn ‘orange’, melyn ‘yellow’, gwynnrudh ‘pink’. Purple is blue plus something, and orange is that same something plus yellow, so rudh must be ‘red’. Pink is that red plus gwynn, so gwynn is ‘white’ (and indeed krogen wynnrudh shows it mutated after a feminine noun). ‘Head’ is penn, from penn daras ‘lintel’ and war grogen benn ‘on a skull’. Put them together in Cornish order, noun first: penn gwynn ‘white head’ - which is the popular etymology of the English word penguin.
